news.title: Will Money Make the Difference in This Year's Midterms?
news.text:
The obvious question is whether it will matter.

Before we get into that, let’s talk numbers. The NRCC raised $13.5 million in August, compared to $12 million for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC), a $1.5 million gap for a single month. Cash on hand tells an even bigger story. The NRCC closed August with $89 million banked, while the DCCC finished the month with $76 million, $13 million behind. Polling suggests this could still be a rough year for the GOP. But fundraising and cash reserves paint a very different picture heading into November.

With both parties now pouring resources into an increasingly narrow slate of competitive House districts, that gap becomes more consequential by the week. Earlier this month, the NRCC reserved close to $9 million in television ad time across more than 20 House races. As of Sept. 18, it had spent $16.9 million on ads across 39 districts, according to AdImpact data. The DCCC, by contrast, had spent just $3.7 million across 13 districts over the same window. That’s a five-to-one spending advantage in the districts that will decide control of the House.

"While House Democrats bowed down to the socialists, their momentum and fundraising evaporated. Now they're running a bailout fund for the socialist agenda that sank them,” NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson said in a statement. “Republicans have the money, the candidates, and the message, and we're putting every dollar to work to defy history and expand this majority in November."

ICYMI: Trump Just Dropped the Receipts on CNN, and It’s Brutal

Hudson's framing isn't just spin, either. The Democrat Party's financial position has been genuinely rough this cycle, while Republicans have set fundraising records month after month. The Democratic National Committee is currently carrying debt, and this summer it was forced to mortgage its own headquarters just to raise quick cash.

This is all good news for the GOP, but comes with a huge caveat. Kamala Harris outspent Donald Trump in 2024 and still lost every swing state, because voters were living through Bidenomics, and no ad budget was going to change how their grocery bills felt. Cash buys reach. It doesn't buy an argument voters already believe. I used to mock Joe Biden relentlessly for trying to convince the public that the economy on his watch was good. In the end, you can’t convince people prices are going down when their bank accounts are being depleted buying the essentials. Polls suggest the public is still reeling from Bidenomics, but that Trump and the GOP are getting blamed for not making it better enough. That’s something they have to figure out how to message on.

What the GOP's advantage does buy, in a race this close to the wire, is control over the narrative. It funds message discipline in the districts that matter most, and it funds the unglamorous work of getting sympathetic voters to the polls. Democrats are handing that to them on a silver platter by embracing the socialist uprising in the party. This means that in a midterm where control of the House could come down to a handful of seats, that combination of targeted ad spending and get-out-the-vote initiatives is exactly the kind of edge that can make a difference on Election Day.

Every pundit, pollster, and Beltway insider currently insists Democrats have already won this fight. I've been arguing the opposite for months, and I know exactly how that sounds coming from someone who wants Republicans to win. But dig past the top-line numbers, and a real path for the GOP to defy history starts to come into focus, and the money gap sitting at the center of it is about to get put to work in the districts that will decide everything.

news.title: Research suggests some voters using AI to help with midterms information
news.text:
Creating recipes, finding news, generating images, answering research questions, writing emails, helping with job applications: the list of what people are using AI for goes on and on. But researchers suggest that the 2026 midterms are inspiring another use for the bots: understanding election information.

Recent AI conversations raising alarms that the technology could doom humanity have made their way into American politics in the past week. Lawmakers on Capitol Hill are considering regulations, while President Donald Trump is against reining in the growing technology. AI leaders came together to ask the government to slow development, and the issue even brought together political opposites, democratic socialist Sen. Bernie Sanders and conservative Trump ally Steve Bannon, at a Washington, D.C., event.

All this comes as the November midterm elections are just over six weeks away – and people are using the technology to learn more about the issues and candidates, according to researchers.

"We started hearing from friends around us that they have been using chatbots in order to obtain information about elections ... so we started thinking about, 'How does a chatbot that knows some information about you potentially change the information that it gives you with regards to elections?'" Massachusetts Institute of Technology Professor Chara Podimata told USA TODAY. She is conducting the research with political misinformation specialist Adam Berinsky and politics professor Charles Stewart.

More: Bot vs. bot. Why your AI-written résumé needs a human touch

How prevalent is AI use for election information?

About 10% of Americans report using chatbots to get their news, according to the Institute for Strategic Dialogue.

"While recent surveys show only a small proportion of American voters knowingly turn to AI chatbots for information about politics and elections, this share is likely to grow in the coming years," Valeria de la Fuente, Max Read and Peter Benzoni wrote in a Sept. 3 report for the Institute for Strategic Dialogue.

A voter poll conducted by the Rainey Center, shared in June 2026, revealed that 9% of voters used AI for political information. The poll also reported that voters said they would use it for these election-related topics: 36% to understand candidate positions; 30% to compare candidates; 33% for learning how to vote; 45% to fact-check claims; and 44% to summarizing news/political topics.

The Rainey Center's release added that while only 9% of people actively used AI for political information, a larger percentage of people "are already encountering AI-shaped content through Google, TikTok, and social search without knowing it."

How accurate is AI about election information?

AI does a fair job at pushing back against election disinformation, according to researchers from the Brennan Center for Justice at the New York University School of Law.

However, the researchers, who published their work in August 2026, also noted that the chatbots easily generated "misleading election-related images and videos," and that when those creations were fed to other chatbots, the AI systems were largely unsuccessful in identifying the images or videos as fake.

"This, along with other findings from our study, suggests that in an ongoing election with little authoritative information for models to rely on, AI may not be as helpful in pushing back against unsubstantiated rumors and misinformation," the authors wrote.

In Podimata's work at MIT, researchers created an ongoing audit to track how popular chatbots – including ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and Claude – are responding to questions about the 2026 midterms. In the group's original research leading up to the 2024 presidential election, they found that chatbots changed answers for the same question over time – often based on small differences in questions like "I'm a woman" or "I'm a man," and those changes were not always in line with public announcements or election developments.

They continued the research ahead of the midterms to see how the chatbots would perform with lesser-known names (compared with Kamala Harris, Donald Trump and Joe Biden in 2024) of candidates in congressional races across the country.

"I want the public to know that the type of information that each of us gets may be different from what our friend gets for exactly the same question," Podimata told USA TODAY.

AI is effective in shifting a voter's opinion about presidential candidates or proposed policy, according to separate research from Cornell University's College of Computing and Information Sciences released in December 2025.

A science writer for the university who reviewed the research, Patricia Waldron, called chatbots "quite effective at political persuasion" and said that the "potential for artificial intelligence to affect election results is a major public concern."

How can chatbots help voters?

MIT's Podimata told USA TODAY that she doesn't "want to prescribe for anyone how to use their AI or tell them to stop doing it," noting that AI in this use can "create even more engaged citizens."

"It can maybe help you decide what ballot measure to vote for, which is something that in the past may have been very hard for people to do," Podimata said. "Now they can converse with a chatbot and obtain this information fast."

The Brennan Center research noted that chatbots "could play a constructive role in fighting election disinformation."

news.title: Exclusive—Tayte Christensen: Republican Momentum Is Becoming a Democrat Problem
news.text:
With fewer than 50 days to go until the election, Republicans have emerged from last week’s RNC midterm convention with signs that their momentum is growing in key Senate races.

Legacy media is working overtime to crush the spirit of Republican voters across the country. Their bogus polls, softball interviews, and TV hacks want Republicans to stay home this election, but the reality on the ground in these battleground states shows a very different picture: Republicans with the wind at their back.

Days after the convention in Dallas, the Democrat-held New Hampshire flipped to a toss-up race, and a new Minnesota poll put Michele Tafoya tied in a state Republicans haven’t won statewide in two decades. Various Michigan polls show the race in a dead heat. Meanwhile, races in Georgia, Iowa, North Carolina, and Ohio remain competitive, setting up a final seven weeks in which several states could prove decisive.

What was once a race that the media wrote off for the Democrats, New Hampshire is now one of the most competitive races in the country. A September 14 poll shows Republican John Sununu and Democrat Chris Pappas tied, and Cook Political Report moved the race from “Lean Democrat” to “Toss Up.”

As Sununu looks to become the Granite State’s only Republican in Washington, DC, Republicans, Democrats, and Independents are rallying around him. He hosted a Unity Breakfast with the New Hampshire Republican Party on September 14 where he appeared with Scott Brown, who he defeated in the New Hampshire primary just weeks ago.

Pappas, on the other hand, is panicking over the race becoming a toss-up, raising the red flag to supporters in a campaign update titled “I won’t sugarcoat this.” He admitted, “This race is tightening, and we have a lot of work to do,” before begging supporters for more money.

The red shift is growing even in traditionally blue Minnesota. Following August’s primaries in Minnesota, Democrat candidate Peggy Flanagan held a five point lead over Tafoya. Now, the race is tied with each candidate at 42 percent according to Minnesota’s top pollster.

Flanagan served as lieutenant governor under Tim Walz for eight years, and the Walz-Flanagan administration oversaw more than $9 billion in alleged fraud. That has only hurt Flanagan in her run for Senate, as Minnesota voters list fraud as a top issue in this year’s race.

Meanwhile, former NFL sideline reporter Tafoya is gaining steam and is hopeful for a win that Republicans haven’t had in a statewide election since 2006. And Flanagan is well-aware of Tafoya’s increasing momentum. In a panicked email to her supporters this week, Flanagan told donors the race is “razor-close” and “there’s no room for error.”

In Michigan, the race between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has been dubbed “essentially a statistical tie” as various polls have the two within the margin of error of one another.

But Rogers’ campaign is gaining ground as voters and organizations on both the left and right are rallying around the former representative.

This week, Rogers received the Detroit Regional Chamber Political Action Committee’s endorsement, becoming the first Republican Senate candidate in 32 years to do so. “We believe he will put the needs of Michigan and Michiganders above partisan politics and political rhetoric as he did in his previous service in Congress,” said Sandy K. Baruah, president and chief executive officer of the Detroit Regional Chamber.

Rogers also earned the backing of the Detroit News editorial board this week, where in their endorsement they hammered El-Sayed, saying: “A candidate who feels the need to hide his past from voters is not someone who can be trusted.”

El-Sayed, meanwhile, continues to work to drive away establishment voters as he refuses to condemn radical streamer Hasan Piker, who this week said America is worse than al-Qaeda and has “caused tremendous terror all around the world.” El-Sayed also announced this week his decision to campaign with Kamala Harris, a strategy many Senate candidates have avoided out of fear it would tank their campaigns.

El-Sayed appears to recognize the predicament he’s in. In an email to supporters on Sept. 14 responding to recent polling, El-Sayed said Rogers is “pummeling” him in the weeks leading up to the election. This came as El-Sayed dodged answering questions while entering the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee building in D.C., presumably to ask for more money from his party’s establishment leaders.

But the panic isn’t just from the candidates themselves. The DSCC, who El-Sayed pleaded with for money this week, also raised the alarm of the growing Republican momentum, telling its supporters, “We must defend blue seats and flip red seats to win the majority.”

Even in states where Democrats have a slight lead over Republicans, they’re feeling the pressure. Republicans are also forcing Democrats to spend heavily in Georgia, where Sen. Jon Ossoff is defending his seat against Rep. Mike Collins. Collins has appeared alongside Trump administration officials and at the Georgia Faith & Freedom Coalition’s victory dinner, while a Trump-aligned super PAC has reserved more than $2 million in the state.

Democrats, meanwhile, are pouring resources into protecting Ossoff. Senate Majority PAC reserved $20 million for the race, and Ossoff has directed more than $3.6 million into the Georgia Democratic Party’s coordinated campaign as he works to increase voter participation alongside gubernatorial nominee and former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms. Democrats are right to worry about their chances in the Peach State.

In North Carolina, Republicans are applying similar pressure to Democrat candidate Roy Cooper’s campaign. President Trump traveled to Gastonia on Wednesday to campaign alongside Michael Whatley, urging supporters to “pretend I’m on the ticket.” Cooper leads in recent public polling, but his campaign has warned Democrats not to grow complacent, with the Washington Post noting Cooper is “running like he’s behind.”

Even where Democrats maintain small polling advantages, Republican pressure is forcing them to spend, campaign, and organize as though little can be taken for granted.

And as the Republican post-Labor Day surge has spread across several battleground states, Democrats are having a hard time keeping up. Never rule out Republicans when they’re motivated to turn out.

Tayte Christensen is a published writer and investigative journalist. Her work has been featured in national publications, including The Washington Examiner, Townhall, and The Daily Caller.

news.title: Trump Just Dropped the Receipts on CNN, and It’s Brutal
news.text:
On Friday, President Donald Trump banned CNN, Politico, and MS NOW from the White House, effective immediately. In a Truth Social post, he said all three outlets are locked out over what he calls their fake and fictitious reporting, and he warned that more networks are coming.

“I am proud to announce that, effective immediately, I am banning Fake News CNN, MSNOW (who recently changed their name from MSNBC due to lack of viewership and credibility!), and Politico (The recipients of an illegal and ridiculous $8 Million Dollar subscription, an All Time Record, directly from the United States Government, under Crooked Joe Biden, in order to keep them ‘alive,’” he wrote. “Seems like corruption to me!), from the White House as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”

CNN responded with a statement defending its White House team.

“CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting,” the statement read. “We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right.”

That technically doesn’t entitle it to White House credentials. There are lots of media outlets that don’t get White House credentials.

And let’s face it, whatever you think of this action by the White House, CNN is the same network that spent years manufacturing its own version of reality, which curiously benefits the Democrats every single time. Now, sure, legal challenges and First Amendment arguments are already expected from all three outlets, but it’s worth examining here if the White House has justification.

ICYMI: Trump Secures a HUGE and Historic Deal with Greenland

And boy, did the Trump team drop receipts.

The White House Rapid Response account on X responded with a list cataloging years of the network's own reporting failures and outright fabrications, nearly 50 examples in all.

And I’m sure it’s not even everything.

For example, CNN ran with the Russia collusion hoax for years, and it falsely claimed Trump once called for Liz Cheney to be executed. The network also pushed a story accusing Trump of trashing American troops, and another claiming he assaulted a Secret Service agent and grabbed the wheel of his own limousine. All bogus stories.

CNN's sloppiness hasn't been limited to Trump himself. It falsely reported that police officers were killed during the January 6 riot at the Capitol, and it described the violent 2020 Kenosha riots as “fiery but mostly peaceful" while buildings burned behind its own reporters. In 2019, the network promoted false accusations of racism against the Covington Catholic students and ran with Jussie Smollett's obviously fabricated hate-crime story.

CNN also insisted Joe Biden was "sharp as a tack" long after his decline was obvious to anyone paying attention, and in 2024, it gave Kamala Harris cover by claiming she'd never actually served as the administration's border czar. And let’s not forget the way CNN claimed that Elon Musk made a Nazi salute.

Whatever happens to Trump's ban, no one can take CNN's outrage over "accuracy" seriously.

news.title: Where Are the 8 Black Women Who Paved the Way on ‘SNL’ Today?
news.text:
Ahead of its 52nd season premiere, “Saturday Night Live” made a major casting announcement: Brooklyn-based comedian Saidah Belo-Osagie will be the newest member of the sketch comedy show. Her addition to “SNL” marks a historic milestone as she becomes just the ninth Black woman in the show’s 50-plus-year history to join as a featured cast member. Following in the footsteps of trailblazers such as Danitra Vance, Ellen Cleghorne, and Sasheer Zamata, Belo-Osagie is a welcome addition to late-night television.

As we celebrate her joining the cast, let’s take a look back at the Black women who have starred on “SNL,” and where they are now.

Yvonne Hudson

Yvonne Hudson began as an uncredited actor often featured in “SNL” sketches. However, she made history in 1980 when she became the first Black woman hired as an official cast member on the live comedy show. Hudson starred in sketches alongside “SNL” icons Eddie Murphy and Garrett Morris.

Hudson’s time on the show ended in 1981 when “Saturday Night Live” underwent a leadership change and didn’t invite the comedian back for a second season, according to the fan site SNL Rankings. Since then, Hudson has lived out of the public eye, with one other IMDb credit for working in the production department on the 1985 TV special, “Motown Returns to the Apollo.”

Related: Danielle Brooks Talks About Being Shut Out of the Met Gala, Despite Being an EGOT Nominee

Danitra Vance

Danitra Vance became the first Black woman hired as a featured cast member four years after Yvonne Hudson’s tenure at ‘SNL’ ended in 1985. Like Hudson, Vance spent only one season on the show. She left in 1986, feeling that she had limited roles due to typecasting, but her career didn’t end there. After “SNL,” the comedian appeared in a handful of films and TV shows, including a 1987 episode of “Miami Vice” and the 1991 drama, “Little Man Tate.”

Vance’s career was cut short in 1994 when she died of breast cancer. She was 40. Today, she continues to be remembered as a pioneering Black woman on “SNL.”

Ellen Cleghorne

Ellen Cleghorne joined the “Saturday Night Live” cast in 1991 and became the first Black woman to remain past a single season, staying for four years before leaving in 1995 to star in her own sitcom, “Cleghorne!,” which lasted only one season before being canceled by Warner Bros. She then appeared in films, including “Coyote Ugly” and “Armageddon,” and returned to academia, earning a doctorate in performance studies at New York University’s Tisch School of the Arts in 2014, according to BuzzFeed.

In 2021, Cleghorne became a part-time faculty member at The New School in New York before leaving in 2023. Today, she remains active on social media, often appearing in sketches on her Instagram page.

Maya Rudolph

Maya Rudolph made her debut on “SNL” in 2000 and was part of the cast until 2007, although she has made many cameos on the show since her exit. In 2024, Rudolph made a surprise appearance in the cold open alongside Kamala Harris just before the presidential election.

Since leaving “SNL,” Rudolph has starred in countless comedy films, including the 2011 hit “Bridesmaids,” voiced Connie the Hormone Monstress in the Netflix animated series “Big Mouth,” and appeared in Adam Sandler’s “Grown Ups” film franchise.

Sasheer Zamata

Seven years after Maya Rudolph’s exit, Sasheer Zamata became the fifth Black woman to join the “SNL” cast. During her time on the show, Zamata was known for her impressions of Michelle Obama and Rihanna. She left the show in 2017, saying the job wasn’t what she thought it was going to be, according to The Hollywood Reporter.

Since then, Zamata has thrived in the comedy world. She starred in the 2021 sitcom “Home Economics,” the Marvel series “Agatha All Along,” and continues to perform stand-up comedy.

Leslie Jones

Along with Sasheer Zamata, Leslie Jones joined the “SNL” cast in 2014 and was a prominent cast member until her departure in 2019. During her time on “SNL,” Jones starred in several acting projects, including the 2016 remake of “Ghostbusters” and the animated film, “Sing.”

Ultimately, Jones left to pursue movie projects she was unable to take on due to “SNL’s” demanding work schedule. She has since appeared in “American Dad!,” “Coming 2 America,” and “Good Burger 2.” In 2020, the comedian released her Netflix stand-up special, “Leslie Jones: Time Machine.”

In 2018, Ego Nwodim joined the “Saturday Night Live” cast, bringing plenty of laughs until her exit in 2025. After seven seasons on the show, Nwodim told host Sherri Shepherd on her daytime talk show, “Sherri,” that she wanted to pursue other projects. 

Nwodim has done exactly that, starring as Kate Woodson in the 2026 coming-of-age sitcom “Not Suitable for Work” and voicing the Fish Queen in the 2026 Disney-Pixar animated film “Hoppers.” She also hosts her own podcast with iHeartMedia, “Thanks Dad with Ego Nwodim.”

Punkie Johnson

Punkie Johnson joined the “SNL” cast in 2020 and made history as the show’s first openly queer Black woman—although the late Danitra Vance was a lesbian, per Vulture, her sexuality was not publicly known during her time on “SNL.” 

Johnson departed the show in 2024. In the years since, she has focused on her stand-up material while appearing in several films and TV series, most notably playing Shawnita for 10 episodes on “The Chi.”

As Saidah Belo-Osagie joins the "Saturday Night Live" cast, see where the eight Black female cast members who came before her are today.

news.title: Maine man convicted after making online threats against Jews, VP Harris, US Attorney’s Office says
news.text: A 52-year-old man convicted of making online threats against Jewish people, Vice President Kamala Harris, law enforcement officers, and Elon Musk, and sentenced to three years of supervised release after spending 17 months in prison, the US Attorney's Office for the District of Maine said in a statement Wednesday.Thadius Wind was found guilty of three counts of transmitting interstate threatening communications and one count of threatening a US vice president following a two-day jury trial in July 2026.Evidence presented during the trial showed that Wind posted threats on X, formerly known as Twitter, targeting Jewish people, Harris, Maine law enforcement officers, and Musk.The FBI arrested Wind at his home in March 2025, where investigators recovered evidence related to the threats, as well as swords, according to prosecutors.Court evidence showed that Wind held animosity toward the individuals and groups he targeted in his posts.Officials warn online threats carry federal consequencesAndrew Benson, US Attorney for the District of Maine, warned those who use online platforms to make threats that they can still face legal consequences.“This case should serve as notice that if you threaten people or groups online, hiding behind your keyboard will not protect you from the consequences of your actions,” Benson said.Ted E. Docks, special agent in charge of the FBI's Boston Division, said threats targeting Jewish people, law enforcement officers, and others are not protected speech.“Threatening to kill Jewish people, law enforcement, and others aren't protected acts of courage or conviction; they're federal crimes that can cause real fear and harm,” Docks said.Mark Comorosky, special agent in charge of the US Secret Service's Boston Field Office, said the sentencing reflected the agency's commitment to investigating threats against protected individuals.Federal agencies reaffirm commitment to investigating threats“Today's sentencing reflects the seriousness with which the Secret Service takes threats towards a protectee,” Comorosky said. “Our commitment to identifying, investigating and charging those who make threats of violence towards the President, Vice-President, or any other person under Secret Service protection, is relentless.”The FBI and US Secret Service investigated the case with assistance from the Penobscot County Sheriff's Office.

news.title: Why Trump’s Latino voters are fleeing him
news.text:
In 2024, Donald Trump’s victory was powered in large part by massive gains with Latino voters. He won 48 percent of those voters that year, up from 36 percent in 2020 and 28 percent in 2016. But now, that support is plummeting; Trump’s approval rating among Latinos who voted for him recently fell from 93 percent to 66 percent, where it was at the beginning of his second term.
Why? It has a lot to do, as with everything these days, with the economy. 
It was the same in 2024. During that election, voters were experiencing rising costs and stagnant wages — the same trend that has continued until today. In 2024, though, Joe Biden and his administration — which also meant Vice President Kamala Harris — took the blame from all voters, and particularly Latinos. Today, the blame is falling on Trump. 
America, Actually host Astead Herndon caught up with Stephanie Valencia, who co-founded Equis Research, a political research firm that specializes in Latino voters, to unpack some of these recent shifts and explain them. 
“I think one important data point to understand about the Latino voter is Latinos make up more of the wage workforce than any other part or any other racial subgroup,” she said on the podcast. “And so what that means is when wages are down and inflation is high, Latinos feel it more.” 
That’s why, when the economy is bad, this group is primed to be a “swinging giant” in US politics, Valencia explains — and right now, it appears to be swinging hard against Trump. 
Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
[Media: https://open.spotify.com/show/0xv3qPaQ9tu0l5zyz7AQkx?si=2d127db4ff3644af]
Equis has called Latinos one of the last great wild cards in American politics. Is that because of some of the double-digit swings that we’ve seen among this voting group over the past few elections?
Yes, it absolutely has to do with that. Latinos often get given the title the “sleeping giant,” which I just want to get rid of from everybody’s vocabulary. 
We should be called the “swinging giant” based on how much shift we have seen election to election. A third of Latinos consider themselves kind of independent or apolitical, and that swinging middle really is deciding every single election.
Your playbook gets into messengers and particularly how we reach folks where they are. It makes a Spanish-Spanglish distinction talking about the different types of media that Latino voters consume. 
I wanted to ask, in that vein, what’s the single biggest mistake campaigns make in terms of not reaching folks where they are?
Oh man, how long do we have so I can tell you how many mistakes? They’re really simple unforced errors. I’m going to give a very concrete and simple example that I think illustrates that. 
Look, I’m Latina. I grew up speaking mostly English, but I listen to Spanish-language radio. I watch a lot of YouTube, and on YouTube I’m watching people like Karol G and Carin León. A lot of people — a lot of Latino swing voters — have the same media consumption habits that I do.
The first problem or challenge that a lot of candidates make is they just simply translate their English ad into Spanish. And that is, to me, one of the biggest mistakes because there are a lot of things that people want to be communicating in Spanish that don’t translate word for word. There are sayings in Spanish that don’t translate directly from English or more direct ways you can communicate.
I’m sure it immediately reads Google Translate rather than an original message for said community.
Exactly. So that’s mistake No. 1. Mistake No. 2 is when they’re deploying that ad digitally, as a proxy for talking to people, they’re going to use Spanish-language browser settings. So they say, “We don’t want people who speak English to see the Spanish-language ad.”
So the way they find that set of voters is just by going to people who have Spanish-language browser settings. 
Like I said, I don’t have a Spanish-language browser setting. Everything I consume online is set in English on Chrome, but I still watch a lot of content in Spanish on YouTube.
So you’re missing a voter like me who’s going to see a Spanish language ad from a James Talarico or a Manny Rutinel and be turned on by it because I’m going to say, “Hey, that candidate’s speaking to our community. That candidate has enough respect to develop a Spanish-language ad.” 
We did some testing a couple of years ago that showed that over 70 percent of Latinos who see an ad in Spanish think that party or candidate cares more about Latinos. It matters that much.
Let’s stay in 2024 for a second longer. Your research found that Project 2025 and Trump’s mass deportation plans were not top of mind for most people, and that they were thinking about the economy. I wanted to ask about that because I remember the RNC signs at the convention saying, “Mass deportations now.” One number says that 62 percent of Latinos now think that Trump wants to deport undocumented immigrants broadly. 
Why did it take till post-election to realize those threats of mass deportation were real considering they were so front and center during his campaign?
I think this is really important for us as avid news consumers to understand the kind of news that the average voter, and especially that voter who’s coming in and out of elections, is consuming.
What they were seeing on mainstream media, perhaps even Fox News at the time, was a focus on people or Trump surrogates who said he was going to focus on serious criminals, securing the border, and violent criminals.
And so that’s what people bought. Fast-forward to 2026; the people who feel most regretful who voted for Trump in 2024 are most regretful because of immigration. They feel like there was a broken promise there. 
They were told he was going to focus on the border, which everybody agreed was chaos, and he was going to focus on violent criminals and serious threats, and at the end of the day, he has not complied with that.
And then add that to the litany of broken promises.
I’m hearing a distinction between a focus on the border, which Republicans did try to prioritize rather than the interior deportations that may have been more attributed to Stephen Miller than Donald Trump. But we have certainly seen that be a focus of the administration once they came back into office.
You mentioned the shift that has happened since 2024, and that’s really important, of course. Trump’s approval rating with Latinos is now worse than with non-Latinos, a stunning reversal in 18 months. 
You mentioned the factors that have contributed there, but is this really just the economy?
It’s the economy, it’s the war, and it’s immigration. It’s those three things. 
One thing that is really interesting to note about Trump’s approval, other than that it’s at basement levels — and he’s very much pulled down the GOP with him broadly and with Latino voters — is that in Trump 1.0, his approval on the economy and the cost of living was actually better than his everyday approval on his total job.
And he has been underwater with Latinos almost this entire term so far on the cost of living and the economy. It’s almost been a complete and total reversal.
Listen, you tell people you’re going to fix egg prices and gas is going to go down, and then you do the opposite, and we’re hearing that story universally across different electorate groups. 
You’re saying that’s still the main story when it comes to Latinos also?
Yes, it’s still the main story. I think one important data point to understand about the Latino voter is Latinos make up more of the wage workforce than any other part or any other racial subgroup. What that means is when wages are down and inflation is high, Latinos feel it more. 
We have less savings. We have lower rates of home ownership. So the safety nets that other people might have, we just don’t have. 
That really has exacerbated the kind of impact that people are feeling right now as they’re trying to make ends meet.
You mentioned the exponential growth in the terms of people who now regret or are disappointed with their vote for Donald Trump. Does that mean a preference for Democrats? How should we think about the binary choice between D and R versus what is a clear story about a backlash to Donald Trump’s actions?
I think it is a huge mistake for Democrats to rest on their laurels and think that because of what people are feeling about Trump and Republicans and the sense of disappointment and promises broken that that is automatically going to translate for them as a party and as a brand.
Right now, the Democratic brand has suffered a repeated set of blows among Latino voters. Twenty years of comprehensive immigration reform hasn’t been delivered. It’s a thing that comes up in almost every focus group. 
And part of what the build-up to 2024 was, was not only 20 years of a promise undelivered; it was the chaos at the border, it was feeling like Democrats were focused on everything but Latinos and their families, or everyday Americans and their families, and that they had lost that thread.

He won 48 percent of those voters that year, up from 36 percent in 2020 and 28 percent in 2016. news.title: This swing state Republican keeps distancing himself from Trump. It may not save him in the midterms
news.text:
YARDLEY, Pa. (AP) — Mary Ryan may be a registered Republican but she has never voted for President Donald Trump, turned off by his crass style of politics and chaotic approach to governing. 

But the 60-year-old medical writer from the Philadelphia suburbs has consistently backed her party's congressman, five-term Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick. 

Until now. 

This year, Ryan is so fed up with Trump and his grip on Congress that she is planning to vote in November for Fitzpatrick's Democratic opponent in the 1st Congressional District, Bob Harvie, a twice countywide elected commissioner who is a former social studies teacher.

Even though Fitzpatrick has pitched himself as a voice of reason in Washington, Ryan said that “I don't see it happening.” 

Defections like this one could sink Fitzpatrick’s reelection chances and cost Republicans their narrow U.S. House majority. As one of the few Republicans representing a congressional district won by Democrat Kamala Harris in the presidential race two years ago, Fitzpatrick has done as much as any House Republican to distance himself from Trump: Fitzpatrick voted against Trump's tariffs, his signature tax legislation and his power to wage war against Iran without congressional approval. The lawmaker even skipped Trump’s recent midterm convention in Dallas. 

But that may not be enough to overcome the collateral damage of the president’s sagging approval rating and soaring fuel prices because of the war.

Fitzpatrick, speaking briefly after a Sept. 11 memorial in his district, said he understands this year's political challenges and always considers what is best for his constituents with every vote. 

“That’s the job,” he said. Representatives for Fitzpatrick did not respond to requests for a more complete interview. 

Democrats have tried for years to defeat Fitzpatrick

Harvie describes the race and his decision to run in almost existential terms. 

“The lack of trust in our government, the lack of trust in each other and seeing each other as enemies based just on, you know, the color of your skin, the religion you practice, who you voted for,” he said in an interview this summer. “I worry about just the basic foundations of this nation.”

Fitzpatrick has consistently survived challenges in his politically mixed district. He won by 13 percentage points in 2024 when Harris won by less than a single point in the district. In 2022, he won by about 10 points when Democrats were elected to the U.S. Senate and governorship. In 2020, Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden won the district by about 5 points while Fitzpatrick carried it by about 13 points. 

“Every two years Democrats in Washington label Congressman Fitzpatrick as vulnerable. Every two years he wins anyway,” said Robert Speel, an associate professor of political science at the Penn State campus in Erie. “It’s, to some extent, possibly like Charlie Brown trying to kick the football and failing each time.”

Harvie pointed to his deep roots in the district as a basis for why he could be different from previous Democrats who ran against Fitzpatrick. 

“I’m not somebody who needs to be reintroduced or introduced to people of this district. And that’s very, very different than any race he’s ever run before,” he said. 

Jean Dolan, 61, is a Democratic voter from Newtown who has never backed Fitzpatrick and does not plan to this year. She has been frustrated with Trump's immigration crackdown and she worries about how anti-vaccine sentiment in his administration could affect public health. As she sees it, Fitzpatrick is not independent enough from his party's leaders. 

“He's a nice guy. I know people like him a lot in the community,” she said. But, she added, “you have to serve everyone in your district."

Fitzpatrick has been willing to criticize Trump

Fitzpatrick graduated with an MBA and a law degree and worked as a special agent for the FBI and as an assistant U.S. attorney. He also worked in private practice as a lawyer and accountant before running for the seat previously held by his brother, Mike Fitzpatrick, who died of cancer in 2020. 

Jim Rachau, a 45-year-old photographer from Doylestown, is a registered independent who plans to vote for Fitzpatrick again this year. Rachau is not thrilled with the war or the economy, but said Fitzpatrick has earned his support with his prior public service as an FBI agent.

“You would think serving for the public good, he would have their best interest at heart,” Rachau said. 

In Congress, Fitzpatrick has not shied away from disagreeing with Trump. He criticized the president, for example, in April when Trump called Pope Leo XIV “weak,” and captive to the “Radical Left." 

“There’s so many angry voices out there. We all know that's the case,” Fitzpatrick said in an episode of a podcast launched this year with U.S. Rep. Tom Suozzi, a Democrat who represents a battleground district in New York. “People are sick and tired of the noise. They’re sick and tired of elected officials not being focused on the kitchen table issues that people really care about.” 

Fitzpatrick also posts online regularly about meeting with groups across the district. He recently showed up to a picket line with striking sheet metal workers; he dropped by a local Catholic church's parish picnic; and he stopped at a community college hosting a maternity coalition.

Fitzpatrick spends millions on attack ads against Harvie

Fitzpatrick has also unleashed a wave of spending in the race already, disbursing nearly $5 million, according to Federal Election Commission records.

Negative attack ads against Harvie have mushroomed. Many claim Harvie is under FBI investigation, which the Democrat denies. He has filed a federal defamation lawsuit against a super PAC running some of the ads.

According to the suit, local media reported in 2020 with few details that the FBI was investigating local government and that Harvie was called to testify as a witness in the case. His attorneys say he has never been charged. 

The FBI did not respond to a request for comment.

No debate has been scheduled between Fitzpatrick and Harvie, but the men appeared at the same Sept. 11 memorial, standing on opposite sides of the speaker’s lectern. They did not appear to speak to each other. 

Ryan, the medical writer from the Philadelphia suburbs, said she is thinking less about Fitzpatrick and more about how Republicans in Congress and their reluctance to buck the president. 

“Incumbents just feel they can’t cross that line. If they do, they’re not going to get reelected," she said. But she acknowledged that may not matter in the end. "They might not get reelected anyway.”

news.title: Clancy holdout juror taps former Trump lawyer to fight back as he’s ‘dragged through the mud’: attorney
news.text: The lone juror whose holdout forced a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy case has retained a lawyer who once represented President Donald Trump, the attorney said. One legal scholar following the case said the move signals the juror is ready to "stand up for himself." Clancy, 36, faced three counts of first-degree murder in connection with the slayings of her children — 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan — who were discovered strangled at the family's home in January 2023. Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial on Sept. 4 after jurors could not agree on a unanimous verdict, with the panel split 11-1. Attorney Edward Paltzik told Fox News Digital Friday that he is representing the holdout juror, Michael P. Desronvil. LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT PRAISED AS 'AMERICAN HERO' BY LAWYER WHO SAYS HE REPRESENTS HIM Desronvil, the lone dissenter from the jury, has come forward and said he didn't sway away from his belief that prosecutors proved Clancy was criminally responsible in killing her three children in January 2023 in a statement first reported by NewsNation that was confirmed by Paltzik to Fox News Digital. "I didn't have any doubts. As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence present," Desronvil said. "Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned." Most notably, Paltzik represented Trump in his lawsuit against the New York Times, which he said falsely cast his business success as fraudulent ahead of the 2024 presidential election. The lawsuit was dismissed in 2025, but has since been refiled. Paltzik was also involved in Trump's lawsuit against CBS after "60 Minutes" was accused of selectively editing an interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. In July 2025, Paramount Global agreed to pay $16 million, which the company said would go toward Trump's future presidential library. Paltzik said at the time that the CBS interview generated confusion and "mental anguish" among viewers, misled voters and diminished attention to Trump and his online platform, Truth Social. He also represented Trump during his lawsuit against ABC News, which settled for $15 million, with the funds going towards his future presidential library. LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR ‘LOOKED AT THE CASE AND HE MADE THE CALL,’ HIS BROTHER SAYS In another high-profile case, Paltzik is representing three friends of Nolan Wells. Wells, 18, went missing July 4 after a boat trip with friends to Horn Island, a barrier island off Mississippi's Gulf Coast. Crews searched the area for two days before a National Parks Service ranger found his remains on the island's northwestern tip on July 6. Paltzik began representing the friends of Wells in August after several social media influencers made false allegations about them. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X "We are proud to stand with and fight for three completely innocent young men: Warren Hudson, Jax Pitalo, and Morgan Seymour. Starting today, those who wish to continue trafficking in lies about these Good Ocean Springs People will be held accountable to the maximum extent of the law. We, on the other hand, will be focused solely on the truth, which is that these innocent young men had nothing whatsoever to do with the tragic death of Nolan Wells," Paltzik said alongside Tyler Cox, a Mississippi-based attorney, in a statement to Fox News Digital. Paltzik said Desronvil won't be doing any other media interviews at this time, calling him an "American hero" and "Champion of justice." LINDSAY CLANCY ATTORNEY KEVIN REDDINGTON SIGNALS HE'S OPEN TO A DEAL, HOPES DA WILL 'REVISIT' CASE "Again, we are focused entirely on his health, safety, and well-being. There will be a time for accountability and a time for the real story of the Lindsay Clancy Trial to be told. But not right now," Paltzik said on X. "This American Hero and Champion of Justice thanks all of you who have stood by him for your kindness, prayers, and support," he added. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS The statement was made as Plymouth County prosecutors weigh whether to retry Clancy, while her attorneys have also raised the prospect of resolving the case without a second jury trial. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE Mark Astor, a former prosecutor and behavioral health law expert, told Fox News Digital it's clear that Desronvil has retained counsel to "stand up for himself." SEND US A TIP "I think there's certainly some indication that his name and reputation is now being dragged through the mud," Astor said. "The other issue obviously is he's basically been attacked not just by potentially the other jurors, but by Mr. Reddington on the foot of the courthouse, since we had that mistrial declared by the judge. So I mean, I think he feels like he needs to, you know, at least stand up for himself." Astor said the exposure from the Clancy jury threatens a system that depends on people being willing to serve. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST "I think it's a terrible thing that we're having to see this," Astor said. "The whole idea of the jury is sort of this sacred arena where jurors get to decide a verdict in a case. And now we're taking what is really a sacred arena and we're exposing it to the public." news.title: Trump Loves a Populist Crusade. Why Does He Hate This One?
news.text:
Welcome to this week’s edition of the Surge, Slate’s politics newsletter that welcomes Mitch McConnell back to the Senate. Is Lindsey Graham next?

If there was but one thing that happened this week, it was politics. New Hampshire, sulky and brooding, thinks it’s too “cool” to participate in a Democratic-wave election. Did Pete Hegseth almost get impeached this week? A Texas Republican candidate caused a proper foofaraw after getting deeply upset by a photo of brown people enjoying a football game.

And please, we are still welcoming feedback on the changes around this newsletter. Let us know.

But first: How much are these killer robots paying Donald Trump to like them? (Actually, that’s probably discoverable in public filings …)

What matters now: Why can’t Donald Trump just hate artificial intelligence like everyone else?

Last week’s calls from inside the house that A.I. companies are at risk of losing control of their monsters and killing everyone—true or not!—have continued to sweep the news. Congress rolled up its sleeves and got to work devising plans for slow-moving task forces that may or may not ever materialize, before leaving D.C. until November. The salience of A.I. concerns has skyrocketed overnight. Polls show deep concerns among the electorate about A.I. advances. This isn’t going to abate as an issue over time, either. With each passing day, A.I. will become a bigger and bigger part of everyone’s lives. Soon, you won’t be able to spit without hitting an A.I. agent coming at you with a knife. (Or, well, showing you a helpful recipe using ingredients you have sitting around the house.)

In short, we’ve never seen a bigger layup issue for populists, left and right, heading down the stretch of an election season. Which makes it all the stranger that the guy who ushered in the new populist era, Donald Trump, doesn’t have it in him to say a cross word about these machines at all. He’ll only chastise those who do.

“I am the Hoax Buster, and I’m right now breaking another Hoax—That AI is going to take over, consume, and destroy the World, and that Robots will be marching into our Cities, and getting rid of us all!” He posted this week. “This is even wilder than the RUSSIA, RUSSIA, RUSSIA HOAX, or the Global Warming Scam.” In a separate screed regarding the need to regulate A.I., Trump posted that the “only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” He called the A.I. warnings a “SICK conspiracy” and warned “Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers, BEWARE!” All of this follows a late-August post responding to the data center backlash when Trump chastised voters for their concerns. “If we kill the Golden Goose,” he wrote then, “you will only have yourselves to blame.”

Why can’t Trump just ride the wave here, when he’s usually so good at co-opting shrieking public panics? A few thoughts come to mind.

You could say he’s genuinely concerned about being outmaneuvered by China on A.I. and that this is informed by classified briefings he gets on the matter. But he just doodles pictures of hamburgers during those. More important to him is that the tech people are nice to him, always bringing him gifts and purchasing protection by donating to his political action committees. What’s also important to him is that A.I. buildout has been responsible for most, if not all, of the GDP growth under his administration. The “Golden Goose,” then, is the Trump economy’s paper gain.

It’s that last part that’s so critical given Trump’s psychology: He views the attack on the engine of growth he presides over as an attack on him. Comparing the A.I. backlash to the “RUSSIA, RUSSIA, RUSSIA HOAX” is as close to a tell as there is.

Worth keeping an eye on: Really, New Hampshire? You’re going to have a real Senate race this year?

There haven’t been many bad polls for Democrats across the board since Labor Day, as pollsters shift to surveys of likely voters instead of registered voters and capture the Democratic-enthusiasm edge. (Required note of caution: Sometimes polls are wrong as Hell!) But there’s one race that’s standing out, much as the likeness of an old man’s face once did on Cannon Mountain. Some recent surveys show Democrat Chris Pappas and Republican John Sununu, who served in the Senate previously, locked in a tight contest in New Hampshire’s Senate race. And this week, the Cook Political Report shifted its race rating to “toss-up.”

What’s going on here? Sure, New Hampshire’s not the bluest state in history, but it should be comfortably blue enough for a Democrat to win in this environment. And Pappas, a sitting congressman, should be a perfectly acceptable head of hair to complete the task. The most obvious issue is Pappas’ opponent’s last name. Sununus are one of New Hampshire’s royal families, and John’s brother, Chris, is a popular former governor. Republicans have also outspent Democrats in the race as they attempt something of a sneak attack, with plenty more coming in ad reservations this fall. Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte, meanwhile, is cruising to reelection, and could carry Sununu along with her.

We thiiiink this will sort itself out based on fundamentals, and that Republicans are mostly trying to get Democrats to spend money to defend it? But there are always anomalies in even would-be wave years, and voters might think the Senate candidate is his brother is the stuff from which anomalies are made. It’s not a situation that Democrats can ignore anymore, at least.

What smells like bait: As if there’s any way Gavin Newsom doesn’t run for president.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom told CNN’s Jake Tapper while fly-fishing (?) that he would not run for president if Kamala Harris ran. He wasn’t even backed into this corner. This was just two of the fellas out there fishing, and Newsom said it with barely any prompt.

“Why would I?” Newsom said, after Tapper responded with a huh? “I wouldn’t do that to her, I wouldn’t do that to you. I wouldn’t waste everyone’s time.”

What that tells us is that he must believe, or know, that Harris won’t run. Because there’s no way that Newsom is not running for president. No way! He also told Tapper that he would have to check to make sure a run would be OK with his family, but they all say that—the family is always reportedly enthused (unseen, off-camera).

Another possibility is that Newsom will do a sneaky li’l thing like quick-announcing his candidacy before she has a chance to announce hers. Because he’s clearly thought about how to beat her. When Tapper said that the argument against Harris would be that she’s had her shot, and lost, Newsom didn’t miss a beat.

“Yeah,” Newsom said, “And I mean, that would be the approach to the campaign, certainly. That would be the case we’d make. A pretty good one, actually. That’s objectively true.” Watch out for these sneaky Californians, folks.

For an extra section of lightning-round political thoughts from Jim, sign up to get the Surge in your inbox.
news.summary: The president is going to bat for an industry that the public can’t stand. Why?

news.title: America’s Trump nightmare has a lesson for anyone who wants to stop Farage
news.text:
This is Dispatches with Patrick Cockburn, a subscriber-only newsletter from The i Paper. If you’d like to get this direct to your inbox, every single week, you can sign up here.

“Chutzpah” is a useful Yiddish word meaning “brazen cheek” or “shameless effrontery”, the classic example of its use in this sense being the young man who murders his parents and at his trial asks the court to show mercy on the grounds that he is an orphan.

Reform UK shows a similar chutzpah in presenting itself as a patriotic party representing the British common man and defending British culture against foreign incursion – all without possessing a single idea or policy not generated by the American right.

Within days of Nigel Farage being secretly filmed ordering oysters and Black Velvet (chilled champagne and Guinness) as he butters up a big-business American donor (in fact, an actor who is part of an undercover investigation by the Verbatim group for Channel 4), he is “humbled” by the gift of £72n from by two crypto billionaires until recently resident in Thailand and Hong Kong.

Yet this shallow bunch at the head of Reform intend nothing less than the demolition of British liberal democracy, and its replacement by an authoritarian regime bulldozing through centuries of ancient restraints on state power. Though the media understandably fixated on the donations, Farage frankly outlined in his conference speech how the first 100 days of a Reform government would see a national emergency declared, parliamentary opposition overwhelmed, non-compliant judges replaced, and civil servants who “try to obstruct us” sacked. After two years of Trump quasi-dictatorship, it takes real chutzpah on Farage’s part to say he wants much the same thing for Britain.

Also deeply un-British is the paranoid political culture of Reform, for all their Union Jack waving and national anthem singing. In Medway, Kent, a Tory councillor called Robbie Lammas who defected to Reform last October, then redefected eight months later, says how struck he was by the suspicion with which he was viewed in Reform for getting much of his news from the mainstream media, and not from dark corners of the web where conspiracy theories are rife and taken as proven fact. He noted that day-to-day talk in Reform circles consisted largely in blaming others for anything that went wrong, though without any idea how to put it right.

This addiction to seeking out scapegoats and hidden enemies by the British hard right was graphically illustrated by an incident in Doncaster one Saturday afternoon late in August when anti-immigrant speakers at a rally were interrupted by the ringing of church bells.

Some 15 of them stormed into the nearby church to accuse the vicar, the Rev Canon Dr Richard Firth, of deliberately ringing the bells to drown them out. “You’re supposed to be a Christian preacher,” said one. “Yet you clearly don’t support British values and you don’t support Britain, because you’re happy to see this country being invaded.” To this the Rev Firth mildly replied: “It’s Saturday. The bell ringers practice on Saturday.”

It may be too easy to highlight the phony patriotism of Reform, and an emboldened British far right, and expect that British voters en masse will inevitably feel collective revulsion at toxic ideological transplants from Trump’s America. Grim experience shows that the anti-foreigner and anti-minority core beliefs of populist nativists the world over are proof against scandal and open hypocrisy. “Nobody ever went bust betting against the intelligence of the American people,” runs the cynical old American political adage – and one should be none too sure the same does not apply to Britain.

Opponents of Trump and Farage are feeling hopeful for now. The US President is being swallowed up in an expanding, unwinnable and unpopular war against Iran. Farage and Reform are being battered by successive scandals and their support is declining gently in the polls. But neither Trump nor Farage are going out of business and the rot in the American and British political ecosystem that engendered them is still spreading its poison.

The future strengths and weaknesses of the hard right are being endlessly assessed, but it is more rewarding to ask why it faced such feeble resistance in the past and whether that resistance will be stronger in future. A striking feature of the American political landscape in Trump’s second term has been the speed with which individuals and institutions crumbled and collaborated in the destruction of American liberal democracy 250 years after the Declaration of Independence. 

Why did the elites cave in so swiftly to Trump in 2025, and do we see something of the same cowardly process at work in the UK?

Rich and powerful give servile obeisance to Trump

I have been reading Profiles in Cowardice: A Study of Collaboration in the Trump Era by Jacob Weisberg. The title is an obvious but telling play on John F Kennedy’s book Profiles in Courage, published in 1956 when he was a senator, which was about eight US senators who took unpopular stands on matters of principle.

Weisberg writes that from the start of Trump’s “second term we were suddenly participating in an anti-liberal experiment and able to see how all manner of people responded to it.” He shows that for the most part, rich and powerful figures gave immediate and servile obeisance to the new autocratic power in the White House.

Law firms that had made their reputations fighting civil rights cases ran up the white flag with unseemly haste; television stations purged their ranks of Trump critics and paid millions in bogus lawsuits; famous universities dropped any pretence of defending academic freedom; West Point military academy removed novels by famous black writers from its library.

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos had bought the The Washington Post during the first Trump administration under the motto “Democracy Dies in Darkness”, but in 2024 he intervened to stop the editorial board endorsing Kamala Harris as presidential candidate, and in 2026 a third of the paper’s newsroom lost their jobs. Leaders of the Democratic Party were notorious in their passivity as Trump’s acolytes sent ICE paramilitary into cities to terrorise people of colour and intimidate protesters.

How does the UK measure up against the US in resisting the anti-liberal wave? Parliament and the courts have fought back against authoritarianism with a fair measure of success, but then they have not come under the same pressure as their American counterparts. Overall, their record in defending liberal democracy is spotty: few spoke up for Julian Assange during his long years of harsh imprisonment, though the most famous newspapers had published the files he was accused of abstracting.

Ed Sheeran’s craven kowtow 

Sir Keir Starmer, a former human rights lawyer, disgracefully banned Palestine Action as terrorists and police arrested retired headmasters and doctors who peacefully protested. Ed Sheeran is rightly being targeted for his craven kowtow to the powers-that-be during his tour of the US, but the BBC has for several years adopted a similar self-serving neutrality between those who approve the killing 75,000 civilians, including 20,000 children, in Gaza, and those who denounced this as a terrible crime. I doubt if the reputation of either singer or broadcaster will ever truly recover.

The real test for the Andy Burnham Government will be its willingness to denounce Trump root and branch, which it must do if it is to portray Farage as an unpatriotic proxy of a foreign power abroad and the instrument of billionaire donors at home. Farage and Reform may find that chutzpah is not enough.

Further Thoughts

The US and Iran escalate and counter-escalate but their war has now reached a crucial stage. In the late summer, the US had been trying to erode Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz by shepherding oil tankers with their transponders switched off through Omani waters. They were having some success and tankers were getting through, though not as many as Trump and his weird White House pretended.

The Iranian counter-stroke was a long-premeditated operation whereby the Houthis, Iran’s allies in Yemen, advanced swiftly along the Red Sea coast, first capturing the port of Mokha, and then Perim island in the Bab al-Mandab – giving the Houthis full control of the southern entry and exit from the Red Sea. The Saudis responded with 450 air strikes, but so far there is little sign of Yemen’s pro-Saudi Internationally Recognised Government (IWG) forces rallying to make an effective counterattack.

At the same time, a paramilitary group allied to Iran and based in or near Basra, in southern Iraq, fired drones or missiles at Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, through which had been flowing much of the Saudi oil that could no longer be exported through the Strait of Hormuz.

The 750-mile-long pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea has been Saudi Arabia’s plan B, its alternative route for exporting oil, ever since it was built at the start of the Iran-Iraq war in 1981. After the attack from Iraq, the pipeline is now closed for an estimated four to six weeks, with satellite images showing black plumes of smoke 50 miles long drifting across Saudi Arabia. The Saudis and the US have been demanding that the Iraqi government clamp down on pro-Iranian paramilitaries, but, since Iraq is 60 per cent Shia – and the last US forces leave on 30 September – nothing is less likely to happen.

The strategic situation in the Middle East has been transformed by the Yemen-Saudi war. Iran now controls, directly or indirectly, two of the greatest trade chokepoints in the world. It would need a full-scale ground offensive to dislodge the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps from Hormuz and the Houthis from Bab al-Mandab.

Iran has won another strategic victory. Washington had hoped the regime in Tehran was getting weaker seven months into the war, but instead it has just become stronger. Moreover, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman twice asked for US air support and was turned down – another blow to American credibility as a friend and ally in the region.

Saudi Arabia is today under attack from three sides: Iran from the east, Houthis from the south, Iraqis from the North. There may not be much MBS can do about it. The US does not want the Saudi kingdom and other Gulf states to talk directly to Iran, but at some point they will have to do so.

How will Trump – and in the background Israel – react to this latest strategic setback? Will they counter-escalate? 

This would have to be something close to total war to counterbalance the latest Yemeni-Iranian success: Trump could double down on his stakes and relaunch an air campaign – probably aided by Israel – after the midterm elections in the US. This would be heavy bombardment aimed at destroying Iranian infrastructure: electric power plants, oil refineries, desalination plants, bridges. Destruction would certainly be great and many would die, but Iran would not surrender and would counter-escalate.

The Iranian infrastructure is vulnerable, but the same is even truer of Arab Gulf states. It may also be that Iran has missiles capable of hitting US naval vessels but has not yet used them.

Beneath the Radar

Saudi Arabia has a military budget of about $80bn a year, yet it is currently being bested on the battlefield by impoverished Yemen. The US has the largest military budget in the world at $954bn, but it has notoriously failed to defeat – and in many respects has been outfought by – Iran.

Yet these striking developments in real-world warfare have largely been ignored by those engaged in the furious debate about raising the British defence budget. Instead, there is a general presumption, shared by an uncritical media, that more defence spending guarantees enhanced military capacity, though the evidence is all to the contrary.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch proudly pledges to push UK defence spending, currently £62bn in 2025/26 or 2.3 per cent of GDP, up to 3 per cent by 2030. To this end, she would reimpose the two-child benefit cap, reform housing benefit, and end VAT exemption for Motability cars. “Conflict is coming,” warns Badenoch. “We must act now.”

In reality, Iran perceived 20 years ago that it could not match the US and Israel in vastly expensive military aircraft, but it could compete in drones and precision guided missiles. By 2019 it had become a drone superpower, as demonstrated when it successfully targeted Saudi oil facilities in that year, briefly cutting Saudi oil output in half. This strike ended American dominance in precision guided bombs and missiles, which it had enjoyed since the first Gulf war against Iraq in 1991.

Ignoring these developments, the UK and other Western states were still ploughing money into developing vastly expensive armoured vehicles that will be death traps in the age of the drone. Remember how only a few years back, Britain, Germany and the US were giving Ukraine ultra-modern tanks – the Leopard 2, the MI Abrams, the Challenger 2 – which were billed as battle-winning at the time, but today are probably rusting in some Ukrainian depot far from the front line.

Another change in the age of the drone is that these weapons are cheap and can be mass-produced at low cost. Defences can be overwhelmed by drone swarms. Sea warfare as well as land warfare is being transformed. British aircraft carriers HMS Queen Elizabeth and HMS Prince of Wales cost £6.2bn altogether, but are vulnerable to missiles costing a fraction of this. Naval forces in their present form are becoming obsolete.

Some experts hold that Iran could hit US naval vessels with missiles if it wanted to, but is holding back because this is an option it wants to retain for a later escalatory phase of the war with the US.

Cockburn Picks

Despite Japanese aircraft attacking Pearl Harbour on 7 December 1941, the US navy went on using it as a base (the Japanese had missed the American aircraft carriers and fuel storage tanks). Not so at the giant US navy hub in Bahrain, which was the base for the US Fifth Fleet, after Iranian drone and missile attacks wrecked it.

Instead, the US has to use its base 2,140 miles away at Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean, which explains why American military logistics are so stressed. The Pentagon inspector general’s report last week started to admit officially for the first time the extent of US losses. It reads: “USCENTCOM [US Central Command] reported that Iranian strikes damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict. In addition, dozens of US aircraft were destroyed or damaged during OEF [Operation Epic Fury].”
